lessons.title: Numbers 1-10
lessons.body: In Shona, the numbers from one to ten are the foundation for all counting. Start by memorising these: 1 â imwe, 2 â piri, 3 â tatu, 4 â ina, 5 â shanu, 6 â tanhatu, 7 â nomwe, 8 â sere, 9 â pfumbamwe, 10 â gumi. Notice that some numbers change depending on what you are counting. For example, when counting people, you say 'munhu mumwe' (one person) but for objects you might say 'chinhu chimwe' (one thing). The numbers themselves stay the same, but the noun class prefix changes. For everyday use, focus on the basic forms first. Practice by counting everyday items around you: 'mbudzi imwe' (one goat), 'mombe piri' (two cows), 'huku tatu' (three chickens). In markets like Mbare in Harare or Kariakoo in Dar es Salaam, you will hear these numbers used constantly. When buying tomatoes, a vendor might say 'madomasi mashanu' (five tomatoes). Listen carefully to how the numbers attach to the noun. To master 1-10, repeat them aloud daily. Write them on a piece of paper and stick it on your wall. Use your fingers to count: one finger for imwe, two for piri, and so on. Try counting your steps as you walk: 'imwe, piri, tatu...' up to gumi. Then start again. This repetition builds muscle memory. Also, learn the question 'Mangani?' which means 'How many?' If someone asks 'Mangani?' you can respond with the number. For example, if you have three oranges, you say 'matatu' (three). Remember that numbers are essential for bargaining. If a seller says 'gumi' (ten), you can counter with 'shanu' (five). Practice with a friend: one person holds up fingers, the other says the number in Shona. Do this for five minutes each day. Within a week, you will know 1-10 without thinking.

lessons.title: Numbers 11-20
lessons.body: Once you know 1-10, numbers 11-20 follow a simple pattern in Shona. For 11 to 19, you say 'gumi ne' (ten and) followed by the unit. So 11 is 'gumi neimwe' (ten and one), 12 is 'gumi nepiri' (ten and two), 13 is 'gumi netatu', 14 is 'gumi neina', 15 is 'gumi neshanu', 16 is 'gumi netanhatu', 17 is 'gumi nenomwe', 18 is 'gumi nesere', 19 is 'gumi nepfumbamwe'. For 20, the word is 'makumi maviri' (twenty). Notice that 'makumi' means 'tens' and 'maviri' means 'two' â so literally 'two tens'. This pattern continues for all tens: 30 is 'makumi matatu', 40 is 'makumi mana', 50 is 'makumi mashanu', etc. But for this lesson, focus on 11-20. Practice by counting from 11 to 20 aloud: 'gumi neimwe, gumi nepiri, gumi netatu, gumi neina, gumi neshanu, gumi netanhatu, gumi nenomwe, gumi nesere, gumi nepfumbamwe, makumi maviri.' Repeat until fluent. Use real-life contexts: if you are at a bus terminus and the conductor says 'gumi neshanu' (15), that might be the fare in Zimbabwean dollars or rand. If you are counting people at a funeral, you might say 'vanhu gumi nemaviri' (twelve people). Note that when counting people, 'gumi nemaviri' is used, not 'gumi nepiri', because 'vanhu' (people) takes the 'va-' prefix. So you say 'vanhu gumi nemaviri' (twelve people). Similarly, for money, you might say 'madhora gumi nemashanu' (fifteen dollars). To practice, write down random numbers between 11 and 20 and say them in Shona. Then, listen to Shona radio stations or watch Shona news, and try to catch numbers in the 11-20 range. You can also play a game: toss a ball and count each toss in Shona from 11 to 20. This makes learning active and fun. After a few days, you will be comfortable with these numbers.

lessons.title: Tens and Hundreds
lessons.body: Counting in tens and hundreds is essential for handling money, measuring goods, and telling time. In Shona, tens are formed with 'makumi' (tens) plus the unit. For example, 10 is 'gumi', 20 is 'makumi maviri', 30 is 'makumi matatu', 40 is 'makumi mana', 50 is 'makumi mashanu', 60 is 'makumi matanhatu', 70 is 'makumi manomwe', 80 is 'makumi masere', 90 is 'makumi mapfumbamwe', and 100 is 'zana'. Notice that from 20 onwards, the word 'makumi' is used, and the unit follows. For 100, the word is 'zana'. For hundreds beyond 100, you combine 'zana' with the tens and units. For example, 200 is 'mazana maviri' (two hundreds), 300 is 'mazana matatu', 400 is 'mazana mana', 500 is 'mazana mashanu', 600 is 'mazana matanhatu', 700 is 'mazana manomwe', 800 is 'mazana masere', 900 is 'mazana mapfumbamwe', and 1000 is 'churu' (or 'churu chimwe'). To say a number like 345, you say 'mazana matatu nemakumi mana neshanu' (three hundreds, four tens, and five). This is similar to English but with 'ne' (and) connecting the parts. Practice by writing down numbers and saying them in Shona. For example, 456: 'mazana mana nemakumi mashanu netanhatu'. Start with round numbers: 10, 20, 30... up to 100. Then 200, 300... up to 1000. Then mix them. Use money: if something costs 250 rand, you say 'mazana maviri nemakumi mashanu'. In markets, you will hear prices like 'zana' (100) or 'mazana maviri' (200). When bargaining, you might say 'mazana maviri' and the seller might say 'mazana maviri nemakumi mashanu' (250). Knowing these numbers helps you avoid being overcharged. Also, when counting large quantities like bags of maize, you might say 'mazana matatu' (300 bags). To master this, practice counting by tens: 'gumi, makumi maviri, makumi matatu...' up to 'zana'. Then count by hundreds: 'zana, mazana maviri, mazana matatu...' up to 'churu'. Do this daily for a week. You can also use a calculator to check your pronunciation. With consistent practice, you will handle tens and hundreds with ease.

lessons.title: Counting Objects
lessons.body: Counting objects in Shona requires matching the number to the noun class of the object. Shona has different noun classes, and the number word changes its prefix accordingly. For example, when counting people (class 2), you say 'vanhu vaviri' (two people). For animals like goats (class 9), you say 'mbudzi mbiri' (two goats). For fruits like oranges (class 5), you say 'maranjisi maviri' (two oranges). For long objects like trees (class 3), you say 'miti miviri' (two trees). For small objects like stones (class 7), you say 'matombo maviri' (two stones). The key is to learn the noun class of the object and then use the appropriate number prefix. The numbers from one to five have different prefixes for each class, but from six onwards, the numbers are the same for all classes. For example, 'tanhatu' (six) is used for all classes. So, to count objects, first identify the noun class. Common classes: class 1 (people) â 'munhu mumwe' (one person), 'vanhu vaviri' (two people); class 2 (plural of people) â 'vanhu vaviri'; class 3 (trees) â 'muti mumwe', 'miti miviri'; class 4 (plural of class 3) â 'miti miviri'; class 5 (fruits) â 'ranjisi rimwe', 'maranjisi maviri'; class 6 (plural of class 5) â 'maranjisi maviri'; class 7 (small objects) â 'chinhu chimwe', 'zvinhu zviviri'; class 8 (plural of class 7) â 'zvinhu zviviri'; class 9 (animals) â 'mbudzi imwe', 'mbudzi mbiri'; class 10 (plural of class 9) â 'mbudzi mbiri'. Practice by picking up objects around you and counting them. For example, count your fingers: 'minwe miviri' (two fingers). Count books: 'mabhuku maviri' (two books). Count chairs: 'zvigaro zviviri' (two chairs). At the market, count tomatoes: 'madomasi mashanu' (five tomatoes). Count maize cobs: 'chibage chimwe' (one maize cob), 'chibage zviviri' (two maize cobs). To get the noun class right, listen to how native speakers count. If unsure, you can often use the generic 'chinhu' (thing) and say 'zvinhu zviviri' (two things). But for fluency, learn the specific class prefixes. Make a list of common objects and their noun classes. Practice counting them daily. For example, count the number of plates in your house: 'ndiro imwe' (one plate), 'ndiro mbiri' (two plates). Count the number of cups: 'mukombe mumwe' (one cup), 'mikombe miviri' (two cups). This hands-on practice will make counting objects natural.

lessons.title: Telling Time Basics
lessons.body: Telling time in Shona is straightforward once you know numbers. The basic question is 'Inguvai?' which means 'What time is it?' The answer starts with 'I' (it is) followed by the hour and minutes. Shona uses a 12-hour clock, but you can specify morning, afternoon, or evening. For example, 7:00 is 'I7' or 'Inguva yechinomwe' (the seventh hour). 8:00 is 'I8' or 'Inguva yesere'. To say 7:30, you say 'I7:30' or 'Hafu pashure pa7' (half past 7). But more commonly, you say '7 nehafu' (7 and a half). For 7:15, you say '7 nechikamu chimwe chechina' (7 and a quarter) or simply '7:15'. For 7:45, you say '8 asara maminitsi gumi nemashanu' (15 minutes to 8) or '7:45'. In everyday conversation, people often use English numbers for time, but you can use Shona numbers. For example, 'Iva nemaminitsi mashanu' means 'It is five minutes'. To ask 'At what time?' you say 'Nguvai?' or 'Ini nga ndione' (let me see). Practice by looking at a clock and saying the time in Shona. Start with whole hours: 1:00 â 'I1' or 'Inguva yekutanga'; 2:00 â 'I2' or 'Inguva yechipiri'; 3:00 â 'I3' or 'Inguva yechitatu'; 4:00 â 'I4' or 'Inguva yechina'; 5:00 â 'I5' or 'Inguva yeshanu'; 6:00 â 'I6' or 'Inguva yetanhatu'; 7:00 â 'I7' or 'Inguva yechinomwe'; 8:00 â 'I8' or 'Inguva yesere'; 9:00 â 'I9' or 'Inguva yepfumbamwe'; 10:00 â 'I10' or 'Inguva yegumi'; 11:00 â 'I11' or 'Inguva yegumi neimwe'; 12:00 â 'I12' or 'Inguva yegumi nembiri'. For minutes, you say the hour plus 'namaminitsi' (and minutes). For example, 5:20 is '5 namaminitsi makumi maviri' (5 and twenty minutes). 5:40 is '6 asara maminitsi makumi maviri' (20 minutes to 6). In rural areas, people often use the sun's position: 'Mangwanani' (morning), 'Masikati' (afternoon), 'Manheru' (evening). But for precise time, use the clock. Practice by setting a clock to random times and saying them in Shona. Also, listen to Shona radio for time announcements. Soon, you will tell time confidently.

lessons.title: Using Numbers in Daily Life
lessons.body: Numbers are everywhere in daily life, and using them in Shona will make you more fluent and confident. Start with shopping. In a market, you ask 'Imarii?' (How much?) and the vendor replies with a number. For example, 'Mazana maviri' (200). You can bargain: 'Ndingakupa zana' (I can give you 100). If you are buying multiple items, you say 'Ndinoda matatu' (I want three). At the bus rank, you ask 'Imarii kuenda kuHarare?' (How much to Harare?) and the conductor says 'Mazana mashanu' (500). You pay and say 'Heino mazana mashanu' (Here is 500). When giving directions, you use numbers: 'Famba mamita zana' (Walk 100 metres), 'Tendeuka kuruboshwe' (Turn left), 'Ipa makiromita mashanu' (It's five kilometres). In cooking, you measure with numbers: 'Kapu imwe yehupfu' (One cup of mealie meal), 'Mazai maviri' (Two eggs), 'Mvura ina' (Four waters). At home, you count family members: 'Mhuri yedu ine vanhu vatanhatu' (Our family has six people). You tell your age: 'Ndine makore makumi maviri' (I am 20 years old). You count money: 'Ndine madhora zana' (I have 100 dollars). You use numbers for phone numbers: 'Nomboro yangu ndeye 0771 234 567' â but in Shona, you might say 'Zvirongwa zviviri, zvinomwe, zvinomwe, imwe...' (digits). In farming, you count bags of fertiliser: 'Mabhegi mashanu' (Five bags). You count livestock: 'Mombe gumi' (Ten cattle). In health, you say 'Ndine makore makumi matatu' (I am 30 years old) at the clinic. You measure medicine: 'Mishonga miviri' (Two pills). To practice, make a daily habit of using Shona numbers in real situations. When you buy something, say the price in Shona. When you count items, do it in Shona. When you tell time, do it in Shona. Keep a small notebook and write down numbers you encounter. For example, today you might write: 'Tomato â madomasi mashanu â 50c'. Review your notes. Also, practice with a friend: one person says a number in English, the other translates to Shona quickly. This builds speed. Over time, using numbers in daily life will become automatic.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for the number 3?
quiz.explanation: Tatu is the Shona word for three.

quiz.q: How do you say 'five goats' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Mbudzi shanu means five goats; 'shanu' is five.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 10?
quiz.explanation: Gumi is the Shona word for ten.

quiz.q: How do you say 11 in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 11 is gumi neimwe, meaning ten and one.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 20?
quiz.explanation: 20 is makumi maviri, literally two tens.

quiz.q: How do you say 15 in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 15 is gumi neshanu, ten and five.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 100?
quiz.explanation: Zana is the Shona word for hundred.

quiz.q: How do you say 200 in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 200 is mazana maviri, meaning two hundreds.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 1000?
quiz.explanation: Churu is the Shona word for thousand.

quiz.q: How do you say 345 in Shona?
options: A) mazana matatu nemakumi mana neshanu
B) mazana matatu nemakumi mashanu neina
C) mazana mana nemakumi matatu neshanu
D) mazana matatu nemakumi maviri neshanu
quiz.explanation: 345 is mazana matatu (300) nemakumi mana (40) neshanu (5).

quiz.q: When counting people, how do you say 'two people'?
quiz.explanation: People take the 'va-' prefix, so two people is vanhu vaviri.

quiz.q: How do you say 'three oranges' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Oranges are in class 5, so three oranges is maranjisi matatu.

quiz.q: What is the Shona question for 'How many?'
quiz.explanation: Mangani? means 'How many?' in Shona.

quiz.q: How do you say 'six' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Tanhatu is the Shona word for six.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 7?
quiz.explanation: Nomwe is the Shona word for seven.

quiz.q: How do you say 'nine' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Pfumbamwe is the Shona word for nine.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 4?
quiz.explanation: Ina is the Shona word for four.

quiz.q: How do you say 'eight' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Sere is the Shona word for eight.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 2?
quiz.explanation: Piri is the Shona word for two.

quiz.q: How do you say 'one' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Imwe is the Shona word for one.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 50?
quiz.explanation: 50 is makumi mashanu, five tens.

quiz.q: How do you say 60 in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 60 is makumi matanhatu, six tens.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 70?
quiz.explanation: 70 is makumi manomwe, seven tens.

quiz.q: How do you say 80 in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 80 is makumi masere, eight tens.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 90?
quiz.explanation: 90 is makumi mapfumbamwe, nine tens.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What time is it?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Inguvai? means 'What time is it?' in Shona.

quiz.q: How do you say '7:30' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 7:30 is commonly said as 7 nehafu (7 and a half).

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'morning'?
quiz.explanation: Mangwanani means morning in Shona.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am 20 years old' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 20 years is makore makumi maviri.

quiz.q: In a market, how do you ask 'How much?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: Imarii? means 'How much?' when asking for a price.
